title: Structural Design Patterns
description: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, and Proxy with animated object graphs.

topics.title: Adapter Pattern (Class & Object Adapter)
topics.description: Converting the interface of a class into another interface clients expect.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Adapter Pattern acts as a bridge between two incompatible interfaces, allowing classes with mismatched APIs to collaborate seamlessly.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Reusing legacy libraries or 3rd-party vendor SDKs without modifying their source code.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Wrap the incompatible adaptee inside an adapter class that implements the target interface.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Client calls targetInterface->request(), and Adapter translates it to adaptee->legacySpecificRequest().

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Object Adapter Structure
callout.text: Client -> Target Interface <- [Adapter (has Adaptee)] -> calls Adaptee::legacyMethod()

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: BankPaymentAdapter bridges modern dollars/string interface to legacy cents/char* API.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Payment gateway wrappers, UI graphics compatibility layers, file format converters.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when integrating third-party code whose interface cannot be changed.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use when you have full control to refactor the original API directly.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Separation of concerns; satisfies Open/Closed Principle.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Introduces extra wrapper layer indirection.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Object Adapter (Composition - preferred), Class Adapter (Multiple Inheritance).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Leaking adaptee-specific exceptions through the adapter interface.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between Class Adapter and Object Adapter in C++?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Object Adapter uses Composition (Adapter contains a pointer to Adaptee). Class Adapter uses Multiple Inheritance (Adapter inherits publicly from Target and privately from Adaptee).

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Build an adapter that translates JSON logger calls to a legacy XML printer.

practice.title: XML to JSON Adapter
practice.problemStatement: Build an adapter that translates JSON logger calls to a legacy XML printer.

referenceCode.code: class XmlAdapter : public IJsonLogger { LegacyXml xml; public: void logJson(string j) override {} };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Adapter Pattern (Class & Object Adapter) is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Bridge Pattern
topics.description: Decoupling an abstraction from its implementation so that the two can vary independently.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Bridge Pattern splits a large class into two separate hierarchies: Abstraction (high-level logic) and Implementation (platform-specific execution).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Prevents a Cartesian product explosion of classes (e.g., WindowsCircle, LinuxCircle, WindowsSquare, LinuxSquare = $M imes N$ classes).

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Abstraction holds a pointer to IImplementation: $M + N$ classes instead of $M imes N$.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Shape (Abstraction) holds a pointer to IRenderEngine (Implementation).

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

comparison.title: Class Explosion vs Bridge Solution
rows: WinCircle, LinuxCircle, MacCircle, WinSquare, LinuxSquare, MacSquare

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Shape delegates rendering to IRenderer bridge pointer, decoupling geometry from graphics.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Cross-platform OS windowing (GUI window vs platform window handles), Database drivers.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when you want to avoid compile-time binding between abstraction and implementation.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use when there is only one fixed platform implementation.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Solves combinatorial class explosion; hides platform details.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Increases design complexity with dual hierarchies.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Bridge, PImpl Idiom (specific single-class bridge in C++).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Confusing Bridge with Adapter (Bridge is designed up-front; Adapter retrofits existing code).

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does the Bridge pattern prevent Cartesian product class explosion?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: By decoupling abstraction and implementation into two orthogonal hierarchies linked via composition, turning M * N subclasses into M + N independent classes.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Build RemoteControl abstraction with TV and Radio device implementations.

practice.title: Device and Remote Bridge
practice.problemStatement: Build RemoteControl abstraction with TV and Radio device implementations.

referenceCode.code: class IDevice {}; class Remote { std::shared_ptr<IDevice> dev; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Bridge Pattern is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Composite Pattern (Tree Hierarchies)
topics.description: Composing objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies, treating individual objects and compositions uniformly.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Composite Pattern lets clients treat individual leaf objects and complex branch compositions uniformly through a shared interface.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Hierarchical tree structures (e.g. File systems with Files and Folders, or UI view hierarchies) need recursive operations without custom type checks.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Both Leaf (e.g. File) and Composite (e.g. Directory) implement IFileSystemNode.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: A composite contains a std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Component>> and delegates operations recursively to its children.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Composite Recursion
callout.text: Directory::getSize() -> loops through children -> sums child File::getSize() + nested Directory::getSize() recursively!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: File (Leaf) and Directory (Composite) both implement IFileSystemItem with recursive size summation.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: DOM Trees in web browsers, UI Widget layouts, 3D Scene Graphs.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use whenever representing tree structures where leaves and branches share common operations.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if leaf and branch operations differ radically and cannot share an interface.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Simplifies client code; easy to add new component types.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Hard to restrict which children can be added to specific composites at compile time.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Safe Composite (add/remove on Composite only), Transparent Composite (add/remove on base).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Modifying children list during recursive iteration.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between Safe and Transparent Composite?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Transparent Composite defines child management (add/remove) in the base interface (leaves must throw). Safe Composite defines child management only in the Composite class (type safety).

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement Composite for graphic shapes (Dot, Circle, and CompoundGraphic).

practice.title: Graphic Shape Grouping
practice.problemStatement: Implement Composite for graphic shapes (Dot, Circle, and CompoundGraphic).

referenceCode.code: class Compound : public IShape { std::vector<std::shared_ptr<IShape>> children; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Composite Pattern (Tree Hierarchies) is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Decorator Pattern
topics.description: Attaching additional responsibilities to an object dynamically without subclassing.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Decorator Pattern wraps an existing object dynamically to add new behavior without altering the original class code or using class inheritance.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Inheritance is static and causes class explosion when combining features (e.g. SimpleCoffee, MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, WhipCoffee, MilkSugarCoffee = $2^N$ classes!).

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: The Decorator implements the same interface as the wrapped object AND contains a pointer to it.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Coffee* drink = new SugarDecorator(new MilkDecorator(new SimpleCoffee())).

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Decorator Stacking
callout.text: SugarDecorator -> wraps -> MilkDecorator -> wraps -> SimpleCoffee. Cost: $0.20 + $0.50 + $2.00 = $2.70

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: MilkDecorator and CaramelDecorator wrap ICoffee dynamically, summing descriptions and costs.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Java / C++ I/O streams (e.g. BufferedInputStream(GZIPInputStream(FileInputStream))), UI Scrollbars, HTTP Middleware.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when you want to add capabilities to individual objects at runtime without subclassing.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use when the component interface is huge with dozens of methods.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Adheres to Open/Closed and Single Responsibility principles; dynamic composability.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Hard to remove a specific decorator from the middle of the wrapper stack.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Dynamic Decorator, Static Compile-Time Decorator (Templates).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Assuming object identity remains identical after wrapping.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why is Decorator preferred over subclassing for multi-feature combinations?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Subclassing creates $2^N$ static classes for $N$ optional features. Decorator requires only $N$ decorator classes composed dynamically at runtime.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Build an EncryptedLogDecorator wrapping a basic FileWriter.

practice.title: Encrypted Log Decorator
practice.problemStatement: Build an EncryptedLogDecorator wrapping a basic FileWriter.

referenceCode.code: class EncryptDecorator : public IWriter { std::unique_ptr<IWriter> w; public: void write(string s) override {} };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Decorator Pattern is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Facade Pattern
topics.description: Providing a unified, simplified higher-level interface to a complex subsystem.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Facade Pattern provides a simple, clean interface to a complex subsystem of interacting classes, masking internal complexity.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Clients should not need to orchestrate 15 low-level audio, video, codec, and network classes just to play a video.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Create a single high-level Facade class that encapsulates calls to all subsystem objects.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: HomeTheaterFacade.watchMovie("Inception") turns on projector, dims lights, lowers screen, and starts audio amp.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Facade Boundary
callout.text: Client -> [HomeTheaterFacade] -> coordinates [Amplifier, Projector, Screen, DvdPlayer, Lights]

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: HomeTheaterFacade orchestrates multiple low-level subsystems behind a single watchMovie() call.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Database connection pools, Compiler subsystems, OS SDK wrappers.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when you want to provide a simple default entry point to a complex framework.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if client code needs fine-grained access to low-level subsystem internals.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Reduces client coupling and shields callers from subsystem refactorings.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Can turn into a God object if too many responsibilities are routed through it.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Opaque Facade, Transparent Facade (allows access to low-level subsystem if needed).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Forcing all access through the facade when advanced clients need low-level control.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between Facade and Adapter?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Adapter makes two existing incompatible interfaces work together. Facade defines a brand-new simplified interface for an entire complex subsystem.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Build a ComputerFacade coordinating CPU, Memory, and HardDrive boot sequence.

practice.title: Computer Boot Facade
practice.problemStatement: Build a ComputerFacade coordinating CPU, Memory, and HardDrive boot sequence.

referenceCode.code: class ComputerFacade { CPU cpu; RAM ram; public: void start() { cpu.boot(); ram.load(); } };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Facade Pattern is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Flyweight Pattern
topics.description: Minimizing memory usage by sharing fine-grained intrinsic state among thousands of objects.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Flyweight Pattern reduces memory footprint by sharing common immutable state (Intrinsic State) across thousands of objects, passing dynamic context (Extrinsic State) as method parameters.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Rendering 1,000,000 trees in a forest game will crash RAM if each tree stores its own 50MB 3D mesh and texture.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Split state into Intrinsic (shared TreeType mesh/texture) and Extrinsic (unique x, y coordinates).

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Flyweight Factory caches and shares TreeType instances.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic State
callout.text: Intrinsic (Shared Flyweight): Tree Mesh, Texture, Bark Color (Stored ONCE in RAM)\nExtrinsic (Context): X, Y Coordinates, Current Age (Passed as parameters)

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: TreeFactory shares a single 50MB TreeType flyweight across 5 tree instances.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Word processor text glyph formatters, game particle engines, CSS styling engines in browsers.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use when an application instantiates millions of objects and memory usage is a bottleneck.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use if objects have completely unique, non-shareable state.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Massive RAM savings; improves CPU cache locality.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Increases CPU computation if extrinsic state must be recalculated on the fly.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Text Glyph Flyweights, Particle Flyweights.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Storing mutable extrinsic state inside the shared flyweight class.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: What is the difference between Intrinsic and Extrinsic state in Flyweight?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Intrinsic State is constant, immutable, and shared (stored in the Flyweight). Extrinsic State varies by context and is passed to the Flyweight by caller methods.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Implement BulletFlyweight sharing sprite texture across 10,000 bullets.

practice.title: Game Bullet Particle Flyweight
practice.problemStatement: Implement BulletFlyweight sharing sprite texture across 10,000 bullets.

referenceCode.code: class BulletType { public: string sprite; }; class Bullet { int x, y; shared_ptr<BulletType> type; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Flyweight Pattern is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.

topics.title: Proxy Pattern (Virtual, Remote, Protection)
topics.description: Providing a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Proxy Pattern provides a surrogate object that controls access to the original object, enabling lazy loading, caching, logging, or security access control.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Directly loading a 4K video or connecting to a remote server on startup wastes resources if never accessed.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: The Proxy implements the same interface as the RealSubject, intercepts requests, and delegates when authorized.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Virtual Proxy (Lazy Initialization), Protection Proxy (Auth check), Remote Proxy (Network RPC).

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Virtual Proxy Lazy Loading
callout.text: Client -> ProxyImage::display() -> If realImage == null: new RealImage() -> realImage->display()

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: ImageProxy postpones expensive 500MB disk read until display() is explicitly invoked.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Smart Pointers (C++ smart pointers are proxies!), gRPC client stubs, Spring security proxies.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use for lazy initialization, caching, access control, and remote RPC stubs.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not use when direct access without interception is sufficient.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Saves system resources; provides transparent access control.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Adds latency on the initial intercept call.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Virtual Proxy, Remote Proxy, Protection Proxy, Smart Reference Proxy.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Infinite proxy loops when proxy intercepts calls to itself.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does a Proxy differ from a Decorator?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Decorator adds new dynamic behavior without changing interface. Proxy controls access, lifecycle (lazy load), or security to the underlying object.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Build an AccessProxy that blocks non-admin users from calling executeShutdown().

practice.title: Protection Proxy Auth Check
practice.problemStatement: Build an AccessProxy that blocks non-admin users from calling executeShutdown().

referenceCode.code: class AuthProxy : public IAdmin { string role; public: void shutdown() { if(role == 'admin') real->shutdown(); } };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Proxy Pattern (Virtual, Remote, Protection) is essential for advanced Low-Level Design interviews.
